text: Margaret Emilia Gardiner OBE (22 April 1904 – 2 January 2005) was a radical modern British patron of artists and lived in Hampstead, London, from 1932, where she was also a left-wing political activist. She was briefly the partner of Professor John Desmond Bernal, with whom she was known as "Mrs Bernal" for most of her life, though they were never married. In the 1980 Birthday Honours, she was awarded an OBE for services to the Pier Arts Centre Trust, Stromness, and was listed as Margaret Emilia Gardiner Bernal. Born in Berlin, she was the daughter of Sir Alan Gardiner, an Egyptologist who assisted Howard Carter and Lord Carnarvon in opening Tutankhamun's tomb in 1923, and Hedwig (née von Rosen), Lady Gardiner, whose father was an Austro-Hungarian Roman Catholic with Jewish roots and mother a Swedish Finn; her brother was Henry Rolf Gardiner. She was educated at the Fröbel School in Hammersmith, Bedales, and Newnham College, Cambridge, where she studied Modern Languages before transferring to Moral Sciences (Cambridge's term for Philosophy). Her family was wealthy, so she did not need to work and instead dedicated her life to politics and the arts. At Cambridge, she fell in love with Bernard Deacon, a scholar at Trinity, who died at age 24 from blackwater fever while working in Malakula, New Hebrides (Vanuatu), in 1927; she visited his grave 56 years later and wrote the book *Footprints on Malekula: Memoir of Bernard Deacon* in 1984. After Cambridge, she briefly worked as a primary-school teacher in Gamlingay before focusing entirely on supporting her friends, including Barbara Hepworth, Ben Nicholson, W. H. Auden, Berthold Lubetkin, Solly Zuckerman, and Naum Gabo. She lived at 35 Downshire Hill, Hampstead, near the Heath, where she swam in the ponds into her 90s. Her son with Bernal was Martin Bernal, author of *Black Athena*. Bernal married Agnes Eileen Sprague on 21 June 1922, the day after receiving his BA, and had two children with her and one with Margot Heinemann. With Bernal, a Communist, she was part of the 1930s and 1940s campaign for "Intellectual Liberty," though she was not pressured to join the party. She spent a winter with Bernal in Moscow but had reservations about Joseph Stalin. In the 1960s, she organized full-page advertisements in *The Times* signed by prominent figures opposing the Vietnam War and was a supporter of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND). In the 1970 general election, Ben Whitaker, Labour MP for Hampstead, lost his seat due to a far-left candidate whom Gardiner had financed. She spent much of her life in Rousay, Orkney, as a retreat. In 1979, she founded the Pier Arts Centre in Stromness. One of the gallery's works is "Curved Form (Trevalgan)" by her longtime friend Barbara Hepworth, created in 1956—named after a hill in Cornwall between Zennor and St Ives and Hepworth's first entirely bronze work—which Gardiner kept on display in her back garden in Hampstead. She donated 67 artworks to the people of Orkney, and "Curved Form" now stands outside on the centre's pier on the original plinth from her garden.
